title: Zero-G: A Pre-Decoder-Aware Decoder for Quantum Error Correction
authors: Peter Wegmann, Theofilos Augoustis, Aleksandra Świerkowska, Emmanouil Giortamis, Pramod Bhatotia
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires classical decoders that keep pace with the underlying hardware, translating syndrome measurements into corrections fast enough to avoid an exponential backlog. To meet this real-time constraint, pre-decoders have emerged as part of a hierarchical decoding approach to resolve simple, local errors before passing a sparser residual syndrome to a strong decoder. While pre-decoding should, in theory, speed up the strong decoder, in practice, the speedup is only marginal, since existing strong decoders are designed to decode dense syndromes and cannot exploit the sparsity provided by pre-decoders. To address this, we present Zero-G, a strong decoder designed for use alongside pre-decoders. As a stochastic approximate minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) decoder, Zero-G exploits sparse residual syndromes, dynamically trading latency for accuracy rather than relying on an all-or-nothing runtime-accuracy trade-off. By decoupling hardware control from the decoding core itself, we enable heterogeneous deployment across both FPGAs and CPUs without maintaining separate implementations. Zero-G achieves a $10\times$ latency improvement over existing strong decoders at matching accuracy, with worst-case sub-350ns decoding at code distances up to d=15, while scaling to 640 logical qubits on a single 128-core CPU and 32 logical qubits on a single AMD Versal V80 FPGA.
summary: This paper introduces Zero-G, a novel strong decoder designed specifically for use in hierarchical Quantum Error Correction (QEC) pipelines. It addresses the bottleneck of existing decoders by exploiting sparse residual syndromes passed from pre-decoders. By using a stochastic approximate MWPM approach and decoupling hardware control, Zero-G achieves substantial latency improvements critical for building scalable, fault-tolerant quantum computers.
main_problem: Achieving fault-tolerant quantum computation requires classical decoders that operate in real-time to prevent an exponential backlog of undecoded syndrome measurements.
main_result: Zero-G achieves a 10x latency improvement over existing strong decoders at matching accuracy, while scaling effectively across both CPU and FPGA hardware platforms.
method: The authors propose Zero-G, a pre-decoder aware strong decoder that uses a stochastic approximate Minimum-Weight Perfect Matching (MWPM) approach to exploit syndrome sparsity dynamically.
model_or_system: The work focuses on Quantum Error Correction (QEC), specifically referencing the surface code structure used to encode logical qubits across physical qubits. The system involves a hierarchical decoding pipeline: pre-decoder $ightarrow$ Zero-G strong decoder.
key_observables: Logical Error Rate (LER) and Decoding Latency; the goal is to maintain LER matching with MWPM while drastically reducing latency.
important_parameters: Code distance ($d$), which dictates the scale of the problem, and the required real-time decoding budget ($\approx 1\ \mu	ext{s}$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that a pre-decoder-aware decoder can effectively exploit syndrome sparsity to improve performance beyond what current dense-syndrome decoders can achieve.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the hierarchical decoding process, showing how pre-decoders filter errors and how Zero-G integrates into the pipeline, achieving significant speedups over state-of-the-art methods.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the real-time constraint of QEC, critiques existing decoder limitations (especially regarding syndrome sparsity), introduces Zero-G as a solution, details its stochastic MWPM approach and decoupled hardware architecture, and presents performance benchmarks demonstrating massive latency improvements.
why_interesting: While focused on digital quantum computing, the core challenge—managing complex, time-sensitive information processing pipelines with resource constraints—is relevant to modeling open quantum systems where measurement feedback must be fast enough to stabilize dynamics.
